definition: Undulate means to move in a smooth, wavelike motion.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word undulate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know undulate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: All night the green curtains of the aurora undulated above the fjord.
To tremble is a faint, shivering motion — it stops short of undulate, which rolls in full, smooth waves.
Churn goes further than undulate: undulating water rolls in even waves, while churning water boils over itself in violent confusion.

A ripple is a small surface wave -- undulate on a miniature scale, the teacup version. Both motions travel, but ripple stays tiny and local: a pebble's rings, a shiver across a pond. When the wave runs full-length through a field or a flag, the word is undulate.

To sway is one body rocking side to side -- a mast, a dancer, a drunk -- with no wave travelling through it. Undulate needs the wave itself: motion that moves along a length, section after section. A lamppost sways in the wind; the wheat field undulates.

To roll is the broad heave of a whole mass moving at once -- the deck tilts, the fog bank advances as one body. Undulate is motion in successive waves, each section rising as the last falls. The sea rolls under a ship; an eel undulates through it.

Undulate means to move in a smooth, wavelike motion.
Wind moved through the barley in long pulses until the whole hillside undulated — one slow wave chasing another toward the fence line.
Undulate is the smooth, continuous, full-length wave — a flag, a jellyfish, a wheat field — never a jerk or a wobble.
And note the disguise: the un- is not a prefix.
The word is Latin unda, 'wave,' plus endings; nothing is being negated, and there is no 'dulate' underneath.
Undulate is halfway literary — reach for it when motion travels in smooth waves along a whole length: fields, flags, eels, hills (even a road's dips can undulate).
Ripple is smaller, sway is side-to-side, wobble is unsteady.
For choppy violence, churn.
